ECE 6390 / Navigation

GPS orbit geometry

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how inclined orbit planes provide navigation directions across the sky.

The illustrative constellation uses inclined medium-Earth orbits with a period near half a sidereal day. Inclination carries satellites north and south of the equator while their orbital motion changes longitude relative to a rotating observer.

Visibility is a geometric line-of-sight condition. Positioning quality also depends on directional diversity: nearly redundant measurement directions can constrain some position components poorly.

The six-plane, four-satellite-per-plane arrangement is a teaching geometry. Its ideal horizon counts do not represent the current operational constellation or include terrain and practical elevation masks.

Example

Half of an approximately 86,164 s sidereal day is about 43,082 s, or 11.97 hours. This period accompanies motion across an Earth-fixed observer's sky.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. Why can four well-spread visible satellites give stronger position geometry than four satellites clustered close together?

    Consider which directions of receiver displacement change the measured ranges distinctly.

    Spread directions produce more independent range constraints. Clustered lines of sight can make some displacement and clock-error effects resemble each other, increasing uncertainty despite the same measurement count.
